name: Termius
tagline: Cross-platform SSH, SFTP and port-forwarding client with synced hosts, keys and snippets.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The protocol is free and already on your machine: Termius is a nicer face on OpenSSH, not a network you are locked into. An agent can absolutely build you a host manager TUI that reads ~/.ssh/config, groups hosts, stores snippets, and shells out to ssh and sftp in one sitting, and for a desktop-only workflow that covers most of the daily loop. Where it falls apart is everything past your laptop: a polished iOS and Android SSH client, encrypted cross-device vault sync, port-forwarding UI that does not make you think, and team credential sharing with SSO. If you SSH from your phone at 2am, keep paying. If you SSH from one desk, you were arguably already done before you started.
coreLoopDIY: A terminal host manager that parses your SSH config, lets you fuzzy-search and launch connections, and runs saved command snippets on the selected host.
requirements: OpenSSH client and sftp on PATH
optional: git remote plus age or gpg if you want encrypted vault sync
whatYouLose: Native mobile clients, which is the single biggest reason people pay
Encrypted vault sync across desktop, phone and tablet with conflict handling
A friendly UI for port forwarding, jump hosts and SFTP transfers
Team features: shared credentials, audit trail, SSO, SCIM
Someone else's problem when a key, agent or keychain integration breaks
moatNotes: The moat is client engineering across four operating systems plus a mobile app store presence, not data. Nothing about your hosts belongs to them, which is why leaving is annoying rather than impossible.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because SSH from a phone is genuinely hard to replicate and nobody wants to hand-roll an encrypted sync layer for credentials. Termius also removes a category of small daily friction: remembering which jump host, which key, which tunnel, and it does that identically on every device you own. For teams there is the compliance-adjacent story of shared credentials with an audit trail, which is a different product than a pretty terminal. Solo developers on one machine are the group most likely to realize they were paying for a config file.
notes: The honest version of this build is a TUI that admits OpenSSH already won.
prompt:
Build a terminal SSH host manager and launcher called "portal". Single Go binary, no server, no accounts, no telemetry.

Stack: Go 1.22+, Bubble Tea for the TUI, Lip Gloss for styling, kevinburke/ssh_config for parsing. No other UI frameworks, no web layer.

Behavior:
- On start, parse ~/.ssh/config including Include directives. Build a host list with Host alias, HostName, User, Port, IdentityFile, ProxyJump.
- Full-screen list with fuzzy filter as you type. Arrow keys or ctrl+n/ctrl+p to move.
- Enter: suspend the TUI, exec the real ssh binary for the selected host, restore the TUI cleanly on exit. Do not reimplement SSH, always shell out.
- "f" on a host: prompt for local port, remote host, remote port, then run ssh -N -L in the background and track it in a "tunnels" view where "x" kills it.
- "s" on a host: open sftp for that host in the foreground.
- "g" on a host: pick a snippet from snippets.toml and run it via ssh host "command", streaming output into a pager view.
- "t": tag the selected host. Tags are stored in ~/.config/portal/tags.toml and shown as a filterable sidebar group.
- "r": ping/TCP-dial port 22 for every host concurrently with a 2s timeout, show a green/red dot per host. Cache results for the session.
- Recently used hosts float to the top, tracked in ~/.config/portal/history.json.

Out of scope, do not build: any mobile client, any cloud sync, any credential storage (keys stay in ~/.ssh and the agent), any team sharing, any password prompts of your own.

Optional single extra command: "portal sync" which commits ~/.config/portal plus ~/.ssh/config to a git repo whose remote is read from PORTAL_SYNC_REMOTE in .env. Encrypt nothing yourself, refuse to run if any private key would be included.

Deliver: main.go plus small packages, a Makefile with build and install targets, a sample snippets.toml, and a README with keybindings and a note that this is a wrapper around OpenSSH, not a replacement for it.
